passage: It took me eleven weeks to write one email. Amma thought a stable firm was a gift, and I felt guilty just thinking about leaving. I listed my reasons on paper: the work no longer taught me anything, and I dreaded Mondays. I told Sunaina, my team lead, before anyone else, and "Nitin, are you sure?" was all she said. I gave six weeks' notice, wrote a handover document for each client and trained Arjun on the reports. I was afraid, and on the last Friday relief came first, then a lump in my throat as the team clapped. Guilt still surfaces when Amma asks about my plans, but I would rather remember that I left with the folders in order.

qa.q: How many weeks' notice did Nitin give?
qa.a: Nitin gave six weeks' notice.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Nitin have on the last Friday?
qa.a: Relief first, then a lump in the throat, on top of fear and lingering guilt about Amma's hopes.

qa.q: What steps made Nitin's leaving graceful?
qa.a: Telling the team lead first, giving six weeks' notice, writing handover documents and training Arjun.

qa.q: How might Amma see Nitin's decision?
qa.a: Probably with worry about security, since Nitin says Amma thought a stable firm was a gift.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who feels guilt, fear and relief about leaving and handles reasons, timing and handover carefully.

passage: Supervisor's note, Sudha. Sachin asked to speak after the field team left today. He said he wanted to leave the survey project by the end of April, and he apologised three times in five minutes. He looked relieved to have said it and then scared. He told me his parents expected him to hold a steady job and that he did not want to let the team down. I asked what he wanted to happen before he goes. He proposed finishing the two remaining districts, writing the data-entry guide and training Neha to take over. I agreed the end date in writing, told the director the same day, and set a weekly check-in until the handover is done. I also told him his reasons sounded well thought through.

qa.q: How many times did Sachin apologise in five minutes?
qa.a: Sachin apologised three times in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling once he had said he wanted to leave?
qa.a: Relieved, then scared, and guilty about letting the team down.

qa.q: What could Sachin do in the weeks before leaving?
qa.a: Finish the two districts, write the data-entry guide and train Neha, with weekly check-ins.

qa.q: How does Sudha see Sachin's decision?
qa.a: As well thought through and worth supporting with a written end date and check-ins.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional leaving a project with guilt and fear about family expectations and colleagues, and planning a careful handover.

passage:
At the software company in Noida, Harsha waited outside his manager's cabin with a printed resignation letter. He had rewritten it five times.
He had a new job offer: a smaller company, a role closer to what he wanted. He felt relief when he thought about it. But he also felt guilty. Jatin, his manager, had hired him out of college and taught him most of what he knew. His parents were worried. "Such a big company," his mother kept saying.
Jatin called him in. Harsha's voice wobbled as he explained.
Jatin read the letter and sat back. "I'm sad. But I'm not surprised. You've wanted design work for a year."
"I'll stay the full notice period," Harsha said quickly. "And I've made a handover document for the payments module. I can train whoever takes over."
Jatin smiled for the first time. "That's the part people remember."
Walking back to his desk, Harsha felt his shoulders drop an inch.

qa.q: What had Harsha made for the payments module?
qa.a: A handover document for the payments module.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Harsha have about leaving?
qa.a: Harsha felt relief about the new role but guilt toward Jatin, who had taught him so much, and worry about his parents' fears.

qa.q: What did Harsha do that made the leaving graceful?
qa.a: He told Jatin in person, committed to the full notice period, prepared a handover document and offered to train his replacement.

qa.q: How does Jatin feel about Harsha's news?
qa.a: Jatin feels sad but not surprised, and appreciates the careful handover.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional leaving a job with mixed guilt, fear and relief, who handles the timing and handover gracefully.

passage:
Dear Ganga Paati,
I wanted you to hear this from me, not from Amma.
I'm leaving the firm. I've given notice today, and my last day will be at the end of next month.
I know you spoke to Mr Iyer to help me get this job, and I'm so grateful. That's partly why this took me months to decide. I kept feeling I would be letting you down, and Mr Iyer too.
But I've been unhappy for a long time. The work is all audits, and I want to work on the rural credit programme I read about. I've been offered a place there, starting in January. It pays less, and I'm scared. I'm also relieved in a way I haven't felt in a year.
I've told my team early, and I'm training the junior who'll take my files. I'll write to Mr Iyer myself to thank him.
Please don't worry too much. I've thought about it carefully.
With love,
Lavanya

qa.q: When will Lavanya's last day be?
qa.a: At the end of next month.

qa.q: What feelings does Lavanya describe about leaving?
qa.a: Lavanya feels grateful and guilty toward Paati and Mr Iyer, scared about the lower pay, and relieved in a way not felt in a year.

qa.q: What steps is Lavanya taking to leave well?
qa.a: Telling the team early, training the junior who will take the files, and writing to thank Mr Iyer personally.

qa.q: How might Ganga Paati feel reading this?
qa.a: Paati might feel a little worried but touched to hear it first, and reassured that Lavanya has thought carefully.

grounding: Shows a young professional leaving a job with mixed guilt, fear and relief, attending to family expectations, timing and a graceful handover.

passage:
Nikita, you asked what it was like leaving the water project. I'm Urmila, and honestly, it was the hardest decision I've made.
I'd been there two years. I loved the villages, the women's committees. But the funding had changed, and the work had become mostly reports for donors. I was tired, and I'd stopped feeling useful.
I was scared of what my parents would say. Scared the team would feel I'd abandoned them in the middle of the monsoon season. And, underneath, I felt this huge relief whenever I imagined leaving.
So I didn't leave in the monsoon. I waited till October, when the field work slowed. I told my team lead first, in person. I wrote a handover: every village, every contact, every pending report. I trained Sunita for three weeks.
On my last day, the committee in Khedi village gave me a shawl. I cried the whole bus ride home. Sad, and relieved, both.

qa.q: Who did Urmila train for three weeks?
qa.a: I trained Sunita for three weeks.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel on the bus ride home?
qa.a: Urmila felt sad and relieved at the same time, crying the whole ride.

qa.q: Why was October a wise time for Urmila to leave?
qa.a: Field work slowed then, so leaving would not abandon the team in the middle of the monsoon season.

qa.q: How might the Khedi village committee have felt about Urmila leaving?
qa.a: The committee likely felt sad but grateful, showing it by giving Urmila a shawl.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who leaves a project with mixed fear and relief, and thinks carefully about timing and handover.

passage:
12 August. Nilesh sat in his car outside the bank branch where he'd worked for three years and typed a resignation letter he didn't send. His father had cried with pride when he got this job. His manager, Kavitha, had just trusted him with the new loans desk. He felt sick at the thought of telling either of them, and strangely light at the thought of doing it.
2 September. Nilesh told his parents at dinner that he had an offer from a small design studio. His father put his spoon down. "A bank job is security." Nilesh went through the reasons he'd written down: work he actually wanted, a salary he could live on, savings to cover a few months. His mother said, "Give him time."
3 September. He asked Kavitha for ten minutes. "I'm leaving at the end of the month. I'll finish the loans desk set-up and write everything down for whoever comes next." Kavitha sighed, then nodded. "Thank you for telling me early."

qa.q: What did Nilesh tell Kavitha he would do before leaving?
qa.a: Finish the loans desk set-up and write everything down for whoever comes next.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Nilesh have in the car on 12 August?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty and sick about letting down his father and Kavitha, and at the same time strangely light, relieved at the thought of going.

qa.q: Which parts of how Nilesh left will protect his reputation?
qa.a: Telling Kavitha early, offering to finish the set-up, and writing everything down for the next person.

qa.q: Why might Nilesh's father react to the news as he did?
qa.a: His father sees the bank job as security and was deeply proud of it, so leaving it feels like a risk.

grounding: Shows a young professional deciding to leave a job with mixed guilt, fear and relief, weighing family expectations and handing over carefully.
